links.note: The ribbon is cleaned so the metal itself can combine with oxygen when lit - the burning of magnesium is the chapter's opening combination reaction (2733). The coating being removed is a corrosion product, but what the item is for is the reaction that follows.
Electrolysis of acidulated water splitting one reactant into two gases in a 2:1 volume ratio - a decomposition reaction (2735); 2736 would require heat as the agent.
Brown copper turning black on heating is the gain of oxygen to give CuO - the textbook oxidation example (2741), not merely 'two things combining'.
Flushing packets with nitrogen keeps oxygen away - prevention of rancidity (2749). 2748 would be what rancidity is.
H2 and Cl2 combine only in sunlight, because the condition supplies the energy to start the reaction - the role of a reaction condition written over the arrow (2732).
Helium or nitrogen for storing fresh oil - prevention of rancidity (2749).
Fireflies glow because a protein undergoes aerial oxidation with emission of light (2741).
Characteristic tests for CO2, SO2, O2 and H2 - the observations (gas evolved, colour change) by which a reaction is detected (2723).
Burns from freshly slaked quick lime and the question 'why was so much heat evolved' - an exothermic reaction (2734).
A cycle left in the open rusting, and rust-proof paint - rusting of iron specifically (2745), not corrosion in general (2744).
The wall whitens only as Ca(OH)2 combines with atmospheric CO2 to give CaCO3 - a combination reaction (2733).
Rust identified as hydrated ferric oxide (2745).
Ranking K, Ca, Al, Au by reactivity. Filed on 2739 because reactivity order is used in this chapter only to predict displacement; the reactivity series proper belongs to the Metals chapter.
H2S is oxidised because it loses hydrogen - the loss-of-hydrogen half of the oxidation definition (2741), not 2743, since only one half is asked for.
Gold and platinum do not corrode - corrosion as a general attack on metals (2744), with no iron and no rust involved.
Foul smell tells you cheese has gone rancid - what rancidity is (2748), not how it is prevented (2749).

Aluminium foil is safe for food because its oxide layer stops further attack - corrosion and passivation (2744). The packing context is not about rancidity here; the answer is entirely about the metal.
Quick lime plus water gives slaked lime - the chemical change is a combination reaction (2733). The paired items 84855, 84878 and 84890 ask about the heat and sit on 2734.
Nitrogen for storing chips - prevention of rancidity (2749).
N2 + 3H2 to 2NH3 named as a combination reaction (2733).
Temperature rises when CaO dissolves in water - the item's whole demand is that the reaction is exothermic (2734).
Silver chloride and silver bromide in black-and-white photography - photolytic decomposition (2737), not thermal (2736).
CO2 through lime water gives CaCO3 (milky) and then soluble bicarbonate in excess - the combination reaction of the white-wash example (2733).
Aluminium is reactive yet safe for packing because the oxide coating is passive - corrosion and its self-limiting product (2744).
Water boiling without heating when quick lime is added - the reaction is exothermic (2734).
Respiration as slow combustion releasing energy is an exothermic process (2734), explicitly against endothermic as distractor.
Nitrogen for storing fat- and oil-containing foods - prevention of rancidity (2749).
Quick lime is CaO, the reactant of this chapter's combination reaction with water (2733).
